title: The AI Boom's Two Engines
gist: Jason Furman's FRB/US simulations find the US data center buildout (~1.3% of GDP above trend, ~75% imported) has lifted GDP only ~0.3%, while the AI stock boom's wealth effect (households own $7.6T of an $11T excess gain in seven AI stocks) roughly doubles the impact to ~0.6% of GDP and 0.3pp lower unemployment. The boom has kept the trade deficit from narrowing, crowds out housing via higher rates, and the main downside risk lies in AI equity valuations and monetization rather than capex itself.

insights.claim: According to a simulation with the Federal Reserve's FRB/US model, the US data center buildout by itself has raised GDP by only about 0.3 percent and lowered unemployment by about 0.1 percentage point as of Q3 2026, despite being among the largest peacetime investment expansions in US history.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: The macro growth contribution of AI capex is far smaller than headline capex figures imply; don't extrapolate capex dollars into GDP one-for-one.
insights.quote: By the third quarter of 2026, GDP is about 0.3 percent higher than it would have been, and the unemployment rate about 0.1 percentage point lower.
insights.locator: The impact of the buildout on GDP has been limited by how much of it is imported

insights.claim: The AI data center buildout adds little to US GDP mainly because roughly 75% of the equipment is imported (about 90% for computers, 80% for communications equipment, 10% for construction); imports enter investment and subtract via imports, canceling out in GDP.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: The GDP/jobs benefit of AI capex accrues largely to foreign hardware producers; the US gets the spending headline but not the output.
insights.quote: imported equipment shows up as positive investment and as negative imports, which cancel out
insights.locator: The impact of the buildout on GDP has been limited by how much of it is imported

insights.claim: Above-trend US spending on computers, communications equipment and data center construction started in mid-2024 and reached 1.3% of GDP by Q3 2026, of which about 1 percentage point was imported equipment.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Only ~0.3pp of GDP of the AI capex surge is domestically produced value added.
insights.quote: Data center spending above trend reached 1.3 percent of GDP, but about 1 percentage point of that was imported equipment.
insights.locator: The impact of the buildout on GDP has been limited by how much of it is imported

insights.claim: Trade data suggest the import share of the US data center buildout could be even higher than the assumed 75%, which would make its GDP effect smaller still.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Upside risk to estimated import leakage means the domestic growth effect is if anything overstated.
insights.quote: The trade data suggests the import share could be even higher, which would make the effect smaller still.
insights.locator: The impact of the buildout on GDP has been limited by how much of it is imported

insights.claim: If US data center investment holds at the 1.6% of GDP it is on track to reach by end-2026, FRB/US projects GDP about 0.45% higher and unemployment about 0.25pp lower by end-2028; if it keeps growing by another 0.5% of GDP per year, the effects rise to about 0.7% on GDP and 0.35pp on unemployment.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Even an accelerating buildout adds less than 1% to US GDP level by 2028 in the Fed model.
insights.locator: The impact of the buildout on GDP has been limited by how much of it is imported

insights.claim: The total data center plus equipment buildout is about 2.5% of US GDP (roughly $840 billion a year), already surpassing the late-1990s telecom and fiber buildout, and analyst forecasts for future buildout keep rising.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: AI capex is now historically outsized relative to prior capex manias, raising the stakes of any reversal.
insights.quote: about 2½ percent of GDP, or roughly $840 billion a year—has surpassed what we saw during the telecom and fiber buildout
insights.locator: A historic buildout, and a stock market boom to match

insights.claim: Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh estimates the data center buildout will be bigger than the most historic capital expenditure booms, such as the railroads and the telecom/fiber buildout of the late 1990s.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Historical capex-boom analogies (railroads, telecom) understate the scale of the current cycle.
insights.locator: A historic buildout, and a stock market boom to match

themes.theme: Stock wealth effect as main engine

insights.claim: Seven AI-related companies (Nvidia, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Broadcom, Oracle) account for about two-fifths of the increase in US public company value since ChatGPT launched; their value more than tripled while the rest of the market rose by about half.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: US equity gains are extremely concentrated in AI buildout names, making the macro wealth effect hostage to a handful of stocks.
insights.quote: just seven companies account for about two-fifths of the increase in the value of U.S. public companies since ChatGPT launched
insights.locator: A historic buildout, and a stock market boom to match

insights.claim: The seven AI stocks are up about $11 trillion more than if they had kept pace with the rest of the market since ChatGPT (as of September 30, 2026; about $9 trillion as of November 5), and US households own about $7.6 trillion of that excess gain.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Roughly $2 trillion of the AI excess gain evaporated between end-September and early November 2026, already eroding the wealth effect.
insights.quote: measured through November 5, the gain is only about $9 trillion
insights.locator: The stock market boom is even more important than the buildout itself

insights.claim: A back-of-envelope 3% wealth effect on households' $7.6 trillion AI stock gain implies about $230 billion of extra consumer spending, or 0.7% of GDP; FRB/US gives a smaller effect of about 0.4% of GDP by Q3 2026.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: AI-stock wealth effect is a larger demand driver than the capex itself; consumer spending is levered to AI equity prices.
insights.quote: If 3 percent of that is spent (a plausible estimate of the wealth effect), that would be about $230 billion in higher consumer spending, or 0.7 percent of GDP.
insights.locator: The stock market boom is even more important than the buildout itself

insights.claim: Combined, the data center buildout and the AI stock gain have raised US GDP by about 0.6% and lowered unemployment by about 0.3pp, with the Fed's policy rule responding with a federal funds rate about 0.35pp higher.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: The AI boom is part of why policy rates are higher than they would otherwise be; an AI unwind would argue for lower rates.
insights.quote: Together, the buildout and the stock gain raise GDP by about 0.6 percent and lower the unemployment rate by about 0.3 percentage point
insights.locator: The stock market boom is even more important than the buildout itself

insights.claim: If the buildout holds at its end-2026 share of GDP and AI stock gains stay at early-November levels, FRB/US projects GDP about 0.75% higher, unemployment about 0.45pp lower and the funds rate about 0.7pp higher by end-2028.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Lagged effects mean the AI boom keeps pushing the neutral-policy path higher into 2028 even without further gains.
insights.locator: The stock market boom is even more important than the buildout itself

insights.claim: Furman models the AI stock gain as investors expecting higher earnings from these companies rather than accepting lower returns on stocks broadly, so it works through household wealth and not through a lower cost of capital for businesses; other business investment rises only slightly.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: The channel choice matters: the boom's demand effect runs through consumers, not through cheaper financing for non-AI firms.
insights.locator: The stock market boom is even more important than the buildout itself

insights.claim: So far the AI economy is less a story about data centers than about the stock market, and the stock market is also where the macro risk lies.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Monitor AI equity valuations, not capex announcements, as the key macro risk variable.
insights.quote: so far the AI economy is less a story about data centers than about the stock market—and that is also where the risk is.
insights.locator: The future: a smaller buildout would be fine, a stock market fall less so, and broader financial risks are the unknown unknown

insights.claim: US business investment has risen as a share of GDP to its highest level since 1982, but excluding computers, communications equipment and data centers, private investment has fallen from 16.8% of GDP in 2023–24 to 16.1%.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Headline capex strength masks a contraction in non-AI investment; the ex-AI economy is weaker than aggregates suggest.
insights.quote: Excluding computers, communications equipment and data centers, private investment has actually fallen, from 16.8 percent of GDP in 2023–24 to 16.1 percent.
insights.locator: A historic buildout, and a stock market boom to match

insights.claim: Over the past year, cost-adjusted US nonresidential construction excluding data centers and power fell 13%, led by factories (down 22%), offices (13%) and warehouses (13%), while power construction (including oil and gas) rose 6%, likely partly to serve data centers.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Factory construction is collapsing despite reshoring rhetoric; power infrastructure is the one non-AI construction segment growing, partly as an AI derivative.
insights.locator: A historic buildout, and a stock market boom to match

insights.claim: Because the Fed responds to AI-boom demand, higher interest rates create a headwind for rate-sensitive sectors like housing: with backward-looking expectations housing is about 0.3% below its counterfactual, an effect that could triple over the next few years as lagged rate effects work through.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Housing is the main domestic loser from the AI boom; the drag is set to grow with lags.
insights.quote: housing falls by about 0.3 percent from where it would otherwise be—with the effect potentially tripling over the next few years
insights.locator: The stock market boom is even more important than the buildout itself

insights.claim: The buildout alone raises rates only about a tenth of a percentage point in FRB/US because most spending leaks abroad, so crowding out is small; residential investment, at about 3.5% of GDP, is below trajectory but too small to lower overall GDP much.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Import leakage also limits the rate-driven crowding-out from capex alone; the stock wealth effect is what drives most of the rate response.
insights.locator: The impact of the buildout on GDP has been limited by how much of it is imported

insights.claim: The AI demand shocks hit a US economy already at what the Fed considers full employment with inflation above target, so effective monetary policy leans against them, partly via higher rates and partly by output temporarily exceeding potential.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: AI boom is inflationary at the margin and keeps the Fed tighter than otherwise.
insights.locator: The data center buildout is set

themes.theme: AI boom props up trade deficit

insights.claim: Absent the AI boom, the US trade deficit would have fallen meaningfully as a share of GDP, possibly due to tariff increases, to its lowest share since 1998; instead the boom kept it roughly constant.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: The AI boom is masking the trade-balance impact of tariffs; an AI capex slowdown would sharply narrow the deficit.
insights.quote: It would have brought the trade deficit to the lowest share of GDP since 1998.
insights.locator: The AI boom kept the trade deficit from narrowing

insights.claim: US imports of data-center-related goods (including consumer computers) have risen from about 1.25% of GDP before the boom to about 3% of GDP so far in 2026.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Foreign hardware suppliers are the direct macro beneficiaries of US AI capex.
insights.locator: The AI boom kept the trade deficit from narrowing

insights.claim: Viewed through saving-investment identities, the AI boom added about 1.4pp of GDP to investment while saving rose only about 0.1pp, lowering the current account balance by about 1.25pp of GDP.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: AI capex is being financed from abroad, increasing US external funding needs.
insights.locator: The AI boom kept the trade deficit from narrowing

insights.claim: Historically investment booms often come with a stronger dollar as foreign capital flows in, which would reduce net exports beyond the direct import effect; FRB/US simulations show the dollar barely moving, so this effect is excluded.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: The model may understate the trade-deficit effect and the dollar-support from AI-driven capital inflows.
insights.locator: The AI boom kept the trade deficit from narrowing

insights.claim: Under forward-looking expectations (buildout continuing through 2031 and productivity growth up 0.5pp annually from 2027), FRB/US raises the 10-year Treasury yield by about 75bp versus about 13bp under backward-looking expectations, enough to more than offset the stock-market gains and leave GDP slightly lower than with no boom.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: If markets price AI-driven productivity forward, long yields could rise sharply and turn the AI boom into a net drag via housing.
insights.quote: that would raise the 10-year Treasury yield by about 75 basis points, compared with about 13 basis points with backward-looking expectations
insights.locator: How much to trust this: a reasonable baseline, with expectations the big unknown

insights.claim: If financial markets and wage setters turned forward-looking only in 2026, much of the added interest rate increase would arrive without time for it to show up in macro data in a large way.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Rate effects of AI expectations could front-run any visible growth payoff.
insights.locator: How much to trust this: a reasonable baseline, with expectations the big unknown

insights.claim: FRB/US likely understates inflation from the AI boom: a model with richer industrial structure would capture bottlenecks driving surging chip and hardware prices.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Hardware bottleneck inflation is a model blind spot; inflation risk from AI capex skews higher.
insights.locator: How much to trust this: a reasonable baseline, with expectations the big unknown

insights.claim: Macro models like FRB/US typically show small effects even for huge shocks such as tariffs, oil shocks or policy departures, and were estimated largely on calm-period data; Fed staff forecasts leaning on FRB/US famously failed to predict the 2021 inflation surge.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Treat model-based small-impact estimates with caution in tail scenarios, especially for inflation and financial stress.
insights.quote: the Fed's staff forecasts, which lean on FRB/US but add judgment and other models, famously failed to predict the inflation surge in 2021
insights.locator: How much to trust this: a reasonable baseline, with expectations the big unknown

insights.claim: Furman believes the smaller model estimates of AI's macro impact are probably correct, arguing the model lacks public discussion's incentives to exaggerate; still, each tenth of a percent of GDP is about $30 billion.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Narratives of AI as the sole driver of US growth are likely overstated.
insights.quote: the model does not have the same incentives that public discussion has to exaggerate effects
insights.locator: How much to trust this: a reasonable baseline, with expectations the big unknown

insights.claim: Because FRB/US is roughly symmetric, ending the data center boom and losing AI stock gains would shave about 0.5pp off US growth next year and 0.25pp the year after, but nothing resembling a recession.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: An AI unwind is a growth slowdown scenario, not a recession base case, in the Fed model.
insights.quote: shaving about half a percentage point off growth next year and a quarter point the year after, but nothing resembling a recession
insights.locator: The data center buildout is set

insights.claim: The US economy could absorb a smaller data center buildout with little GDP effect because imports and interest rates would fall alongside investment; a broader ~30% stock market fall with the buildout ending would slow growth to about 1.5%, still not a recession per FRB/US.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Equity drawdown, not capex cuts, is the scenario that matters for US growth.
insights.quote: if the buildout ended and the whole market fell by something like 30 percent, then the FRB/US model would predict that growth would slow to about 1½ percent
insights.locator: The future: a smaller buildout would be fine, a stock market fall less so, and broader financial risks are the unknown unknown

insights.claim: Meaningful AI productivity gains are probably a necessary but not sufficient condition for the AI boom to continue; Furman's main worry is the inability to monetize the investments, with public policy changes another risk.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Watch AI revenue monetization, not just productivity data, as the trigger for a boom reversal.
insights.quote: Public policy changes or the inability to monetize the investments—the latter is what I am really worried about—could stop the AI boom
insights.locator: The future: a smaller buildout would be fine, a stock market fall less so, and broader financial risks are the unknown unknown

insights.claim: Signs of an AI-driven productivity increase are beginning to appear but are debatable and small, and are excluded from the simulations.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Supply-side AI payoff is not yet a reliable macro input.
insights.quote: If you squint, you can see signs of it, but they are debatable and not large
insights.locator: The data center buildout is set

insights.claim: Financial-system complexities such as leverage unwinding are largely absent from FRB/US; Furman views them as a tail risk that at worst resembles 2001 (a short, shallow recession) rather than 2007–09.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Tail-risk framing for an AI bust: dot-com style mild recession, not GFC.
insights.quote: at worst more like 2001 (a short, shallow recession) than 2007–09 (a financial crisis), and even that is only a risk
insights.locator: The future: a smaller buildout would be fine, a stock market fall less so, and broader financial risks are the unknown unknown
